extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in P. G. Wodehouse, comic fiction, lyricists and literary technique
extracted.subtask_short: writing comic fiction in Wodehouse style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative features relevant to producing or analysing P. G. Wodehouse-style comic prose, lyrics and farce — focusing on diction, plotting, character ensembles, lyric-setting, and workmanship. Useful for writers, critics, and students studying comic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Edwardian slang, quotations and allusions, and literary techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: He used a mixture of Edwardian slang, quotations from and allusions to numerous poets, and several literary techniques to produce a prose style that has been compared to comic poetry and musical comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine period-appropriate slang with poetic/allusive references and varied literary devices to create a light, musical comic prose voice. Balance is implied — the mixture produces the distinctive Wodehouse tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose musicality / comic-poetry comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Wodehouse's prose style has been compared to comic poetry and musical comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for rhythmic sentences, careful cadence and comic timing in wording; prioritize sentence music and timing as part of humor delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining complex sequences of subordinate clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a writer who was himself a scholar and had had his face ground into Latin and Greek (especially Thucydides) as a boy could sustain the complex sequences of subordinate clauses sometimes found in Wodehouse's comic prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layered subordinate clauses deliberately to create comic piling-up, but be aware this requires syntactic control and classical training (or equivalent practice) to remain readable and funny rather than tangled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive plotting: scenario-first method
rubrics_metrics.description: He would take up to two years to build a plot and write a scenario of about thirty thousand words. After the scenario was complete he would write the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan thoroughly: develop an extensive scenario (large, detailed outline) before drafting the prose. The page gives a concrete metric (~30,000-word scenario) and a prolonged planning period for complex plotting and farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: High workmanship and multiple projects in preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wodehouse worked extensively on his books, sometimes having two or more in preparation simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain disciplined craft and revision habits; concurrent projects and careful workmanship are part of sustained comic production and prolific output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric-writing approach: music-first method
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike his original model, Gilbert, Wodehouse preferred the music to be written first, fitting his words into the melodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing lyrics for musical theatre, compose to pre-existing melodies so words align to rhythm and phrasing; this produces lyrics that integrate tightly with music but may be less effective when read in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate songs/lyrics into the action of the libretto
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting naturalistic stories and characters and attempting to integrate the songs and lyrics into the action of the libretto, these works brought a new level of intimacy, cohesion, and sophistication to American musical comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make songs serve the story and character-development rather than functioning as detached set-pieces; integration improves dramatic cohesion and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring character ensembles and serial comic casting
rubrics_metrics.description: His creations include the feather-brained Bertie Wooster and his sagacious valet, Jeeves; the immaculate and loquacious Psmith; Lord Emsworth and the Blandings Castle set; the Oldest Member; and Mr. Mulliner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a stable repertory of characters and settings (recurring ensembles) so that comedic dynamics, running jokes and reader expectations can be exploited across stories and novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farce and farcical method as a central mode
rubrics_metrics.description: It was Wodehouse's first farcical novel; it was also his first best-seller, and although his later books included some gentler, lightly sentimental stories, it was as a farceur that he became known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fast plotting, improbable complications, mistaken identities and escalating comic crises typical of farce to generate momentum and laughter; farce was central to Wodehouse's popular success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: lightness, amiability and (perceived) flippancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics of Wodehouse have considered his work flippant, but among his fans are former British prime ministers and many of his fellow writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a light, amiable, non-confrontational tone that prioritises wit and comic surface; be aware this can be read as 'flippant' by some critics even while being widely admired for craft and charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of American settings and idiom when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: From his boyhood Wodehouse had been fascinated by America... his articles about life in New York brought him higher than usual fees... he used New York and Hollywood as settings for some of his novels and short stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ authentic local colour and idiom when writing about particular locales (e.g., New York, Hollywood) to enhance credibility and to exploit regional comic opportunities; first‑hand familiarity bolstered Wodehouse's marketability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric durability trade-off: music-fit vs standalone verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Donaldson suggests that this is the reason why his lyrics have largely been overlooked in recent years: they fit the music perfectly, but do not stand on their own in verse form as Gilbert's do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious that lyrics tightly tailored to melodies may sacrifice standalone poetic qualities; decide whether priority is theatrical effectiveness or independent lyricism.
